questions.question: What does `@decorator` written above a function definition actually do?
options: It comments out the function so it never runs.
It reassigns the function name to decorator(func), replacing it with whatever the decorator returns.
It runs the function immediately at import time.
It converts the function into a class.
questions.explanation: @decorator above def func(): ... is exactly equivalent to writing func = decorator(func) right after the definition — the decorator receives the original function and returns whatever replaces it, usually a wrapper.

questions.question: Why is `functools.wraps(func)` used inside a decorator's inner wrapper?
options: It makes the wrapper run faster.
It is required for Python to allow the @ decorator syntax at all.
It copies metadata like __name__ and __doc__ from func onto the wrapper, so introspection still shows the original function's identity.
It automatically adds type hints to the wrapper.
questions.explanation: Without functools.wraps, the wrapped function's __name__ and __doc__ get replaced by the generic wrapper's — functools.wraps copies that metadata across so debuggers, help(), and documentation tools still show the original function's identity.

questions.question: What happens when you call a generator function (one containing yield)?
options: All of its code runs immediately and returns the final value.
It raises a SyntaxError unless called inside a loop.
It returns a generator object immediately; none of the function's code runs until you iterate it or call next() on it.
It runs once and caches the result for future calls.
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function never executes its body right away — it returns a generator object. Code only runs up to the next yield each time next() is called on it or it is iterated.

questions.question: A generator is iterated fully in one for loop, then the SAME generator object is iterated again in a second for loop. What happens the second time?
options: It yields the same values again from the start.
It raises a TypeError immediately.
The second loop produces no values — the generator is already exhausted.
It automatically restarts from a bookmark.
questions.explanation: A generator can only be iterated once; once exhausted (StopIteration raised internally), it stays exhausted. To iterate the same sequence again, call the generator function again to get a fresh generator object.

questions.question: Which two dunder methods must a class implement to work directly in a `for` loop as a custom iterator?
options: __init__ and __str__
__iter__ (returning self) and __next__ (raising StopIteration when done)
__enter__ and __exit__
__len__ and __getitem__ only
questions.explanation: The iterator protocol requires __iter__ (commonly returning self) and __next__, which returns the next value or raises StopIteration once exhausted — that's exactly what a for loop calls under the hood.

questions.question: What does the `with` statement guarantee that a plain try/except block does not give you automatically?
options: It prevents any exception from ever being raised inside the block.
It automatically retries the block on failure.
It calls __exit__ (cleanup) as soon as the block ends, whether it exited normally or via an exception, without needing an explicit finally.
It makes the block run in a separate thread.
questions.explanation: with guarantees __exit__ runs exactly once when the block ends, success or failure — that's precisely what a manual finally does, but with ties it automatically to __enter__/__exit__ so it can't be forgotten.

questions.question: In a class-based context manager, what does returning True from __exit__ do?
options: Nothing different from returning False.
It suppresses (swallows) any exception that occurred inside the with block, so it does not propagate further.
It re-raises the exception with additional context attached.
It restarts the with block from __enter__.
questions.explanation: __exit__'s return value controls whether an exception inside the with block propagates: True suppresses it, and the usual False (or no explicit return) lets it propagate normally — accidentally returning True is a common bug that hides real errors.

questions.question: What does `@contextlib.contextmanager` do?
options: It turns a generator function (with a single yield) into a context manager usable with `with`, without writing a full class with __enter__/__exit__.
It makes a function run faster by skipping validation.
It converts any function into a decorator factory.
It permanently caches a function's return value.
questions.explanation: @contextlib.contextmanager wraps a generator function — code before the single yield becomes __enter__, the yielded value becomes the `as` target, and code after yield (typically in a finally) becomes __exit__ — a much shorter way to write simple context managers.

questions.question: Which scenario is the best fit for a generator instead of building and returning a full list?
options: You need random access to items by index.
You need to process a very large or unbounded sequence of items one at a time without holding them all in memory.
You need the result to be a dict, not a sequence.
You need the function to run exactly once.
questions.explanation: Generators shine when a sequence is large, unbounded, or expensive to fully materialize — they compute (and release) one value at a time instead of allocating a full list up front.

questions.question: What is a decorator factory, like `repeat(times)` used as `@repeat(times=3)`?
options: A decorator that only works on class methods.
A function that takes configuration arguments and returns a decorator, which is itself then applied to a function — three nested layers: factory -> decorator -> wrapper.
Any decorator that uses functools.wraps.
A decorator that can only be applied once per program.
questions.explanation: @repeat(times=3) first calls repeat(times=3), which must return an actual decorator function; that decorator then receives the target function and returns the final wrapper — the extra nesting layer is exactly what lets a decorator accept its own configuration arguments.
